topic: Initialization Overload Resolution for Initializer Lists
explanation:
The core concept is that braced initialization, using curly braces, has a uniquely strong preference for constructors that accept a std::initializer_list parameter. When the compiler encounters a braced initializer for an object, if the class has any std::initializer_list constructors, overload resolution will almost always select one of them. This behavior is distinct from parenthesized initialization, which follows standard overload resolution rules without this special bias.

Scott Meyers' key insight is that this preference is so powerful it can effectively 'hijack' constructor calls. He stresses that this is not a minor rule but a fundamental aspect of overload resolution that can lead to surprising behavior. The compiler will aggressively attempt to match a braced initializer to a std::initializer_list constructor, even if it requires performing type conversions on the arguments, and even if another non-list constructor would be a perfect, conversion-free match for the same arguments.

The mechanics of this process are straightforward but absolute. When resolving a constructor call that uses braced initializers, the compiler first exclusively considers constructors taking a std::initializer_list. If it finds one where all the elements in the braced list can be converted to the list's element type (without narrowing), that constructor is chosen, and the overload resolution process concludes. Only if no suitable std::initializer_list constructor can be found does the compiler fall back to treating the braced arguments as a standard argument list and performing normal overload resolution on the remaining constructors.

In practical terms, this means that adding an std::initializer_list constructor to an existing class can be a breaking change. Client code that previously used braced initialization to call a specific constructor might suddenly, and silently, be rerouted to the new std::initializer_list constructor. This is famously demonstrated by container classes like std::vector, where creating a vector with parentheses to specify size and value is completely different from using braces to specify the initial elements. This distinction forces developers to be deliberate and understand that parentheses and braces are not interchangeable for object creation.

The most common pitfall is the assumption that braced initialization is a universally 'better' or equivalent alternative to parentheses. Developers are often caught off-guard when a call that seems to be a perfect match for a regular constructor is instead routed through an std::initializer_list constructor that requires implicit conversions. Another subtle error is forgetting that this rule can even intercept what looks like copy or move construction if braced syntax is used, further diverging from expected behavior.
practical_example: The classic example is std::vector. `std::vector<int> v(10, 20);` calls a constructor that creates a vector with 10 elements, each with the value 20. In contrast, `std::vector<int> v{10, 20};` uses braced initialization, which is 'hijacked' by the std::initializer_list constructor to create a vector containing exactly two elements: 10 and 20.
keywords: initializer list constructor bias, braced initialization preference, initializer_list overload priority
